title: Balancing academics and co-curricular activities
description: A practical guide for Kenyan school principals on structuring co-curricular activities so they genuinely complement academic performance rather than competing with it.
body:
CBE's emphasis on holistic learner development gives co-curricular activities — sports, music, drama, clubs — a more explicit place in the curriculum than under 8-4-4. Yet many Kenyan principals still experience genuine tension between academic time and co-curricular time, particularly as exam periods approach. Managing this well requires treating co-curricular activity as a genuine contributor to student development and wellbeing, not a competing distraction to be minimised.

The evidence on co-curricular participation and academic performance

Contrary to the assumption that co-curricular time is time taken away from academics, research consistently finds that students who participate meaningfully in sports, arts, or clubs tend to perform as well or better academically than those who do not, provided the balance is reasonable. Co-curricular participation builds discipline, time management, teamwork, and a sense of belonging that supports rather than undermines academic engagement.

Structuring the balance deliberately

Protect co-curricular time in the timetable

Co-curricular activity that only happens "if there is time" after academic demands are met rarely happens consistently. Schools that protect specific, fixed time in the weekly timetable for co-curricular activities — and treat that time with the same seriousness as academic periods — build a more genuine culture of participation than those where co-curricular time is the first casualty of a busy week.

Adjust intensity around assessment periods, don't eliminate entirely

It is reasonable to reduce co-curricular intensity in the immediate lead-up to major assessments. Eliminating it entirely, however, removes an outlet that many students rely on for stress management precisely when they need it most. A moderated schedule — shorter sessions, fewer competitive commitments — during high-pressure periods balances both needs better than an all-or-nothing approach.

A useful principle: Treat co-curricular participation as part of a student's overall development record, not a separate, lesser category. Recording co-curricular achievement and participation alongside academic results in a student's overall profile signals that the school genuinely values it, not just claims to.

Ensuring genuine access, not just token provision

A school that offers co-curricular activities on paper but in practice reserves meaningful participation for a small group of naturally talented students misses much of the developmental value for the wider student body. Structuring activities with multiple levels of participation — competitive teams alongside recreational or developmental groups — extends genuine access to more students.

Managing costs and equity

Co-curricular activities sometimes carry additional costs — equipment, transport to competitions, uniforms — that can exclude students from lower-income families if not managed thoughtfully. Schools that build modest co-curricular costs into the general fee structure, rather than charging separately per activity, ensure that participation is not determined by a family's ability to pay extra.

Recognising co-curricular achievement publicly

Sports and arts achievements celebrated with the same visibility as academic achievements — announced in assemblies, included in prize-giving, communicated to parents — reinforce that the school genuinely values holistic development, consistent with CBE's stated aims, rather than treating academics as the only measure that matters.
